variants.prompt: All $m$ null hypotheses are true. Each test falsely rejects with probability $\alpha$. What is $\mathbb E[V]$ for the number $V$ of false rejections?
variants.explanation: Each rejection indicator has mean $\alpha$, so the expected count is $m\alpha$ for any dependence. The chance of any rejection is a union probability. Identical decisions give $\alpha$, whereas independent decisions give $1-(1-\alpha)^m$. Use the union probability when even one false alarm triggers follow-up.

variants.prompt: Two true-null tests reject on exactly the same event. How does $P(V\ge1)$ (familywise error) compare with one test’s false-positive rate?
choices: Equal to one test’s size
Twice one test’s size
The square of one test’s size
Larger than either size but less than their sum
variants.explanation: Each rejection indicator has mean $\alpha$, so the expected count is $m\alpha$ for any dependence. The chance of any rejection is a union probability. Identical decisions give $\alpha$, whereas independent decisions give $1-(1-\alpha)^m$. Use the union probability when even one false alarm triggers follow-up.

variants.prompt: All $m$ nulls hold. Independent tests each falsely reject with chance $\alpha$. What $\alpha$ gives $P(V\ge1)=a$ for the false-rejection count $V$?
variants.explanation: Independence gives $P(V=0)=(1-\alpha)^m$, so exact control under the complete null uses $\alpha=1-(1-a)^{1/m}$. Bonferroni uses the union bound instead, $P(V\ge1)\le\sum_iP(\text{false reject}_i)\le a$. It remains usable when the tests share data.

variants.prompt: Using per-test threshold $a/m$ to bound the chance of any false rejection by $a$ (Bonferroni) requires independent p-values.
variants.explanation: Independence gives $P(V=0)=(1-\alpha)^m$, so exact control under the complete null uses $\alpha=1-(1-a)^{1/m}$. Bonferroni uses the union bound instead, $P(V\ge1)\le\sum_iP(\text{false reject}_i)\le a$. It remains usable when the tests share data.

variants.prompt: A procedure reports $R$ rejections, of which $V$ are false. What does controlling the false discovery rate at 5% promise across repeated uses?
variants.answer: The expected fraction of rejections that are false, taking the fraction as zero when there are no rejections.
variants.explanation: False discovery rate is $\mathbb E[V/\max(R,1)]$, the average false fraction with zero assigned to an empty result. When every null holds, $V=R$ and the fraction becomes the indicator of any rejection. Use this target when you want a reliable list rather than a guarantee about each flagged item.

variants.prompt: If all nulls hold and $R$ counts rejections, the false discovery rate $\mathbb E[V/\max(R,1)]$ equals $P(R\ge1)$. Here $V$ counts false rejections.
variants.explanation: False discovery rate is $\mathbb E[V/\max(R,1)]$, the average false fraction with zero assigned to an empty result. When every null holds, $V=R$ and the fraction becomes the indicator of any rejection. Use this target when you want a reliable list rather than a guarantee about each flagged item.

variants.prompt: You simulate many equally unskilled trading rules on past data (backtest). Why can the highest measured result look profitable?
variants.answer: Choosing the maximum selects a strategy with unusually favorable estimation noise.
variants.explanation: A backtest simulates a trading rule on historical data. If all candidates have equal true performance, selecting the highest backtest score also selects the largest estimation error. That error is typically positive even when each candidate’s error averages zero on its own. Test the selected rule on data that played no part in choosing it.

variants.prompt: If equally skilled rules each have mean-zero backtest error, the rule picked by the highest backtest score also has mean-zero error.
variants.explanation: A backtest simulates a trading rule on historical data. If all candidates have equal true performance, selecting the highest backtest score also selects the largest estimation error. That error is typically positive even when each candidate’s error averages zero on its own. Test the selected rule on data that played no part in choosing it.

variants.prompt: A holdout hides every row and shows only the error score. How can repeatedly revising your model after seeing scores still overfit it?
variants.answer: Scores convey information about holdout errors and guide the sequence of candidates toward favorable noise.
variants.explanation: Error scores reveal which revisions work on these particular rows. Repeated choices of features, seeds or thresholds can therefore fit holdout noise. Freeze the model and the success rule before opening the final scores to measure performance on outcomes that did not guide development.

variants.prompt: You have a final evaluation set whose scores are hidden. Which action preserves it as a test of a preselected model?
choices: Retune until final scores stabilize
Freeze the rule before opening final scores
Choose the seed by the final score
Set the success cutoff after scoring
variants.explanation: Error scores reveal which revisions work on these particular rows. Repeated choices of features, seeds or thresholds can therefore fit holdout noise. Freeze the model and the success rule before opening the final scores to measure performance on outcomes that did not guide development.

variants.prompt: You issue a forecast at time $t$ for an outcome at $t+h$. What makes an older row eligible for training in this fold?
variants.answer: Whether their predictors and realized labels were available by that origin.
variants.explanation: The forecast origin is when you issue the prediction. The horizon is how far ahead the target is measured. A rolling-origin evaluation repeats the prediction at successive origins and uses only rows whose inputs and training outcomes were available by each origin. Moving the origin lets you mimic deployment at a fixed horizon.

variants.prompt: As forecast time $t$ advances, you can expand the training set while predicting outcomes at $t+h$ for the same fixed $h$.
variants.explanation: The forecast origin is when you issue the prediction. The horizon is how far ahead the target is measured. A rolling-origin evaluation repeats the prediction at successive origins and uses only rows whose inputs and training outcomes were available by each origin. Moving the origin lets you mimic deployment at a fixed horizon.

variants.prompt: At day 100 you train a model. One older row has a target built from price changes on days 98–103. Why exclude that row?
variants.answer: Its realized training target uses days after the evaluation decision.
variants.explanation: A forward return is the fractional gain or loss over a future interval. It becomes a usable training label once the interval ends and its final value is observable, including any reporting delay. If that happens after the evaluation decision, fitting on the row leaks future information even when its start date precedes the split.

variants.prompt: A target measures the asset’s gain or loss over a future interval (forward return). What timestamp governs when it can be used for training?
choices: When the position would have opened
When the input feature was generated
When the full return is observable
When the forecast horizon was chosen
variants.explanation: A forward return is the fractional gain or loss over a future interval. It becomes a usable training label once the interval ends and its final value is observable, including any reporting delay. If that happens after the evaluation decision, fitting on the row leaks future information even when its start date precedes the split.

variants.prompt: A scaler uses $z=(x-\bar x)/s$, with $s$ the sample standard deviation. Why can estimating $\bar x,s$ on all dates leak even with no labels?
variants.answer: Its learned statistics depend on feature values unavailable at the training cutoff.
variants.explanation: The mean $\bar x$ and standard deviation $s$ are fitted parameters. Using later rows to choose them lets the training representation depend on future feature values. Fit transformations on eligible training rows and apply the fixed mapping to test rows to mimic what deployment can know.

variants.prompt: Using $z=(x-\bar x_{\rm train})/s_{\rm train}$ on later test rows can preserve a chronological split.
variants.explanation: The mean $\bar x$ and standard deviation $s$ are fitted parameters. Using later rows to choose them lets the training representation depend on future feature values. Fit transformations on eligible training rows and apply the fixed mapping to test rows to mimic what deployment can know.

variants.prompt: Two models predict the same outcome on date $t$, with losses $L_{A,t}$ and $L_{B,t}$. Why compare them using $d_t=L_{A,t}-L_{B,t}$?
variants.answer: They expose the incremental loss on matched outcomes and can cancel shared shocks to forecast difficulty.
variants.explanation: Pairing compares the models on the same outcome and can cancel the effect of an unusually easy or hard date. In $\operatorname{Var}(d_t)$ the covariance between the two losses is subtracted twice. Serial dependence can remain across dates. Estimate uncertainty for the series of differences rather than using two independent error bars.

variants.prompt: Pairing losses by date as $d_t=L_{A,t}-L_{B,t}$ makes the differences independent across dates.
variants.explanation: Pairing compares the models on the same outcome and can cancel the effect of an unusually easy or hard date. In $\operatorname{Var}(d_t)$ the covariance between the two losses is subtracted twice. Serial dependence can remain across dates. Estimate uncertainty for the series of differences rather than using two independent error bars.

variants.prompt: On date $t$, two models differ in loss by $d_t=L_{A,t}-L_{B,t}$. Why resample runs of consecutive $d_t$ instead of single dates?
variants.answer: Resampling neighboring differences together retains some of the dependence that affects uncertainty in the mean.
variants.explanation: Resampling consecutive dates together (a block bootstrap) retains dependence within blocks and cuts it at the joins. Short blocks can miss covariance between nearby dates. If several days share one shock, treating each day as a fresh replicate can make a weak forecast improvement look much more precise.

variants.prompt: To estimate uncertainty in the mean loss difference $\bar d$, you resample consecutive dates. What breaks if the blocks are too short?
choices: The two models become unpaired
The forecast horizon changes
The loss mean becomes a median
Important lag covariance is lost
variants.explanation: Resampling consecutive dates together (a block bootstrap) retains dependence within blocks and cuts it at the joins. Short blocks can miss covariance between nearby dates. If several days share one shock, treating each day as a fresh replicate can make a weak forecast improvement look much more precise.

variants.prompt: To probe a suspected source of bias, you test a second outcome (negative control). What must be true of that outcome for the check to help?
variants.answer: It should share the suspected bias pathway while excluding the hypothesized causal effect.
variants.explanation: A negative-control outcome should be unaffected by the proposed causal mechanism while sharing the bias you are testing. A positive result can reveal that bias. A clean result has limited reach: it can miss errors that only affect the main outcome, or errors too small for the control to detect.

variants.prompt: A negative-control outcome that shows no effect rules out biases specific to the main outcome.
variants.explanation: A negative-control outcome should be unaffected by the proposed causal mechanism while sharing the bias you are testing. A positive result can reveal that bias. A clean result has limited reach: it can miss errors that only affect the main outcome, or errors too small for the control to detect.

variants.prompt: Model A’s mean loss advantage is $\bar d$ for $d_t=L_{B,t}-L_{A,t}$, mostly from one month. How do you quantify that month’s influence?
variants.answer: Compare paired loss differences by period and recompute the overall result with the influential period omitted as a sensitivity analysis.
variants.explanation: Compare the paired loss differences across periods and recompute the mean with the influential period omitted. Show both estimates. If the advantage disappears, the conclusion depends on that period. Test the improvement on a separate period before relying on it.

variants.prompt: If almost all of a statistically clear mean loss gain comes from one period, the model’s advantage may depend on market conditions.
variants.explanation: Compare the paired loss differences across periods and recompute the mean with the influential period omitted. Show both estimates. If the advantage disappears, the conclusion depends on that period. Test the improvement on a separate period before relying on it.

variants.prompt: A complex model beats a constant forecast. Which second comparison can separate the gain from model complexity from the gain from using inputs?
variants.answer: A simple fitted model using the same eligible features and the same forecast origins.
variants.explanation: Fit a simple model on the same eligible features and evaluate at the same forecast times. It gives the complex model a meaningful comparison. For an ablation, keep evaluation and model selection fixed and refit without the group, so the remaining inputs have a fair chance to replace its information.

variants.prompt: You remove one feature group and refit (an ablation). What stays fixed to isolate the effect of that removal?
choices: The evaluation and model-selection protocol
The fitted coefficients for the remaining inputs
The observed losses after removing the group
The set of rows where the removed group worked
variants.explanation: Fit a simple model on the same eligible features and evaluate at the same forecast times. It gives the complex model a meaningful comparison. For an ablation, keep evaluation and model selection fixed and refit without the group, so the remaining inputs have a fair chance to replace its information.

variants.prompt: Before testing, you set a minimum useful loss reduction $\delta>0$. Why choose $\delta$ before seeing the final result?
variants.answer: It makes the decision depend on a gain large enough to justify adoption and avoids choosing the hurdle after seeing the estimate.
variants.explanation: The threshold represents a benefit worth the extra data, serving or maintenance cost. A narrow interval about a negligible gain can establish a real effect while leaving the upgrade unattractive. Setting the threshold before the final test keeps the adoption rule independent of the observed score.

variants.prompt: A precise estimate of a positive loss reduction below the predefined minimum $\delta$ can justify keeping the simpler model.
variants.explanation: The threshold represents a benefit worth the extra data, serving or maintenance cost. A narrow interval about a negligible gain can establish a real effect while leaving the upgrade unattractive. Setting the threshold before the final test keeps the adoption rule independent of the observed score.

variants.prompt: You train on some stocks and test on different stocks over the same dates. What can make their forecast errors dependent?
variants.answer: Both sets can react to the same market or sector shocks at the same dates.
variants.explanation: An asset is an instrument you can invest in, such as a stock. A common factor is a driver that moves many assets together, such as a market-wide price drop. Training and test assets can therefore share essentially the same shock. Holding out a later block of dates tests whether the model works in market conditions absent from training.

choices: Reshuffle the asset split within each date
Evaluate on later, withheld date blocks
Split each sector into equal asset groups
Bootstrap asset-days independently
variants.explanation: An asset is an instrument you can invest in, such as a stock. A common factor is a driver that moves many assets together, such as a market-wide price drop. Training and test assets can therefore share essentially the same shock. Holding out a later block of dates tests whether the model works in market conditions absent from training.
